newsitem.title: USA: Texas Instruments banking on new chips.
newsitem.headline: Texas Instruments banking on new chips.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc., long seen as a lumbering computer memory chip giant, has changed its image by selling its defence electronics division and gambling its future on high-growth chip products, analysts said.
The Dallas-based company said Monday it was selling its defence unit to Raytheon Co. of Lexington, Mass., for $2.95 billion in cash and turning all its attention to its semiconductor business.

Company executives said the move goes hand in hand with a shift away from memory chips toward "differentiated products" like digital signal processors, which translate speech, sound waves and other data into a computer-readable format.
The chips are used in wireless communications products, modems, digital video and digital light processing -- anything that transmits the sights and sounds of the natural world.

Analysts said the sale of the defence unit would probably dilute 1997 earnings, but said it gives Texas Instruments a dynamic profile after years of being one of the more conservative -- and, at times, uninspiring -- players in the high-tech industry.
"It is going to be much more exciting because they are replacing a stagnant defence contracting business with an exciting growth industry," said Cowen & Co. analyst Drew Peck.

Texas Instruments, founded in 1930 as Geophysical Service, has been a pioneer in electronics. It produced the first commercial silicon transistor in 1954, developed the integrated circuit in 1958 and invented the electronic handheld calculator.

Its revenues from digital signal processors have grown at around 30 percent annually for the last three years and last year took up part of the slack left by plummeting prices for common memory chips, long the company's core product.

Texas Instruments Chairman Jim Adams said the company was already focusing more and more attention on digital signal processors and the strategic shift would be quickened by the divestiture of the defence business, which ran up about $1.8 billion in 1996 revenues but was showing only slight growth.
"We expect to be a leading, premiere electronics company focusing on digital solutions," Adams said.
"This (deal with Raytheon) allows us the resources to proceed ... toward that strategy. ... This frees us up to look to our future," he said in an interview.

Analysts said Texas Instruments' $3 billion in proceeds from the sale will probably be used to pay off some debt and finance greater chip production or acquisitions of rival manufacturers of specialised chips.

"I think we will continue to see a lot of development work in production facilities, whether it is in DSP (digital signal processing) or other new-generation products," said William Conroy, an analyst with brokerage Williams MacKay Jordan & Co.
